newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe rushes to settle truck strike.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe rushes to settle truck strike.

text.p: The French government raced against time on Tuesday to bring a nine-day-old truck drivers' strike strangling France's highways and fuel supplies to an end before it spreads to other sectors.

But while hurrying to broker a deal between the truckers and their employers, the centre-right government was wary of setting a precedent on pay or early retirement that could whet appetites among other workers during a period of budget austerity.

The dispute began to hit the franc on foreign exchange markets on Tuesday, dealers said. The French currency lost ground against the dollar and the mark as traders, recalling last year's damaging 24-day public transport strike, weighed the risk of wider labour unrest.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said Prime Minister Alain Juppe's administration was doing its utmost to help reach a deal and would take responsibility for easing earlier retirement for drivers and reducing payroll taxes for employers.

"The negotiations must be concluded within 24 hours," Labour Minister Jacques Barrot told a news conference. "I would be very dismayed if ulterior motives led some people to bet on a failure of these negotiations."

Barrot did not say who he meant, but ministers were worried about statements by Force Ouvriere (FO) trade union leader Marc Blondel, the man who spearheaded last year's strike, threatening to extend the truckers' dispute to other transport sectors.

Communist CGT union leader Louis Viannet said in a television interview: "It is in the truckers' interest to exert the maximum pressure, to make the employers understand that they will gain nothing by digging in their heels."

Five rail workers' unions urged their members on Monday to support the truck drivers "by all appropriate means", but France's biggest union, the Socialist-led CFDT, warned against extending the conflict, saying it would forfeit widespread public support for the truckers.
The divided unions have failed to mobilise public employees for major strikes despite repeated efforts since September.

There was also concern in government circles that road haulage employers, who complain of severe pressure on delivery times from clients and fierce competition from European rivals, were taking a hard line on pay and hours, knowing Juppe was under pressure to bail them out.

Official mediator Robert Cros said he had put forward government proposals to reduce social charges on employers who reduced working hours and facilitate early retirement in exchange for the recruitment of young drivers, and the parties had asked for time to study them.
The government has also pledged to ban all trucks from French roads on Sundays, a measure that previously did not apply to foreign trucks in transit.

The drivers are demanding retirement at 55 instead of 60, a 10 percent pay rise and a cut in working hours, as well as payment for all hours worked, including loading time and compulsory rest periods while on the road.

The risk for the government is that encouraging pay rises or conceding retirement at 55 to truckers would lead to demands from other unions and raise pressure from car manufacturers who are seeking government aid to cut 40,000 jobs through voluntary early retirement.

While the cost of such measures might not have much immediate impact on the state budget -- French media estimates range from one to two billion francs ($200-400 million) for the truckers -- they would add to France's long-term problems in financing pensions while remaining economically competitive.
